title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
Problem setting (from the previous page): a difference of curve lengths, CN−AM, has been reduced to a·√m·∫_0^1 √(1−u²)/√(1−mu²) du. This is a complete elliptic-type integral, related there to a conic arc. Its parameter is m = 2n²/(2+n²) ≡ 2k/(1+k). Two series expansions are being compared. The page carries the marker '(J. A. Euler)', so the hand may be Johann Albrecht's.

Method II. Put u = sin φ. Then 1 − m sin²φ = ((2−m)/2)(1 + k cos 2φ), with k = m/(2−m), so
CN−AM = a√(k/2) ∫_0^{π/2} (1+cos2φ)(1+k cos2φ)^{−1/2} dφ.

This page does the following.
(i) It completes the table of power-reduction formulas: the constant term of cos^{2j}2φ is (2j−1)!!/(2j)!!, and the cos2φ-coefficient of cos^{2j+1}2φ is 2·(2j+1)!!/(2j+2)!!. Both entries shown, cos^6 and cos^7, are correct.
(ii) Since ∫_0^{π/2} cos 2λφ dφ = 0, only these coefficients survive. This gives
∫_0^{π/2}(1+k cos2φ)^{−1/2}dφ = (π/2) Σ [(4j−1)!!/(4j)!!]·[(2j−1)!!/(2j)!!] k^{2j}
∫_0^{π/2} cos2φ (1+k cos2φ)^{−1/2}dφ = −(π/2) Σ [(4j+1)!!/(4j+2)!!]·[(2j+1)!!/(2j+2)!!] k^{2j+1}.
(iii) Adding the two:
CN−AM = (π/2) a √(k/2) · Σ c_n k^n, where c_n = (−1)^n (2n−1)!!/(4^n ⌈n/2⌉! ⌊n/2⌋!), i.e. 1 − k/4 + 3k²/16 − 15k³/128 + …
(iv) As n→∞, k→1 and m→1, so CN−AM → a. This yields 1 − 1/4 + 1·3/(4·4) − 1·3·5/(4·4·8) + … = 2√2/π (≈0.9003).

The 'vicissim' part then tries to sum this series directly. Set k = z². Split the series as s − t: s contains the even powers z^{4j} and t the odd ones z^{4j+2}.
- Termwise differentiation gives (zt)' = s'/z and (z²t)' = z³(zs)'.
- Eliminating s' gives s = (1−z⁴)t'/z + (2−z⁴)t/z².
- Differentiating this and substituting gives (on the next page) the linear second-order ODE z²(1−z⁴)t'' + z(1−5z⁴)t' − (4+3z⁴)t = 0.

In modern terms:
- s = ₂F₁(1/4,3/4;1;k²).
- t = (k/4)·₂F₁(3/4,5/4;2;k²).
- The ODE is the hypergeometric equation in the variable x = z⁴, with indicial exponents ±2 at z = 0.
- Combining with the direct evaluation, the page implicitly contains the quadratic transformation ₂F₁(1/4,3/4;1;k²) − (k/4)₂F₁(3/4,5/4;2;k²) = (1+k)^{−1/2} ₂F₁(1/2,1/2;2;2k/(1+k)).
- At k = 1 this gives 2^{−1/2}·4/π, consistent with 2√2/π.

The next page continues: it reduces the ODE to a Riccati equation, then derives Euler-integral (beta-type) representations of s and t.
errors: No computational errors found: the cos^6 and cos^7 Fourier coefficients, both coefficient series, the general term, the value 2√2/π, the differential relations, the elimination formula for s, and the resulting ODE all check.

Gap: k=1 lies on the circle of convergence (singularities at k=±1). The series converges there only conditionally, with terms ~ 1/(π√2·j) in magnitude. Passing to the limit is an Abel-type step that is not justified, though the result is correct.

Gap in the 'vicissim' programme: s and t separately diverge logarithmically at z=1, since ₂F₁(a,b;c;1) with c−a−b=0 diverges; the next page's integral ∫z²dz/(1−z⁴) at k=1 shows this. So finding s and t separately cannot give the value at z=1 without handling the cancelling divergences. This is not addressed on this page or the next.

ideas.what: Expanding (1+k cos2φ)^{−1/2} binomially and averaging powers of cos over a quarter period to get series for a complete elliptic integral
ideas.modern_name: Series for Legendre function P_{−1/2} / complete elliptic integral via Laplace-coefficient-type expansion
ideas.where_published: Similar expansions appear in Euler's papers on the perimeter of the ellipse and on planetary perturbations (exact Eneström numbers unsure)

ideas.what: Evaluation 1 − 1/4 + 1·3/(4·4) − 1·3·5/(4·4·8) + … = 2√2/π from the geometric limiting case
ideas.modern_name: Special value of a hypergeometric combination on the boundary of convergence (equivalent to ₂F₁(1/2,1/2;2;1) = 4/π)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss summation theorem (1812) for the underlying value
ideas.where_published: unsure; it appears here in Opera postuma (1862) fragments

ideas.what: Splitting the series into even and odd parts s, t and deriving first-order coupled differential relations, then a second-order linear ODE
ideas.modern_name: Hypergeometric differential equation (in the variable z⁴) for ₂F₁(3/4,5/4;2;z⁴)
ideas.where_published: Institutiones calculi integralis vol. II (general method of finding ODEs satisfied by series)

ideas.what: Implicit identity equating the s−t combination with the elliptic integral in modulus m = 2k/(1+k)

missed.claim: Comparing the two expansions of the same integral (in m on the previous page, in k = m/(2−m) here) amounts to a quadratic transformation of hypergeometric series. In modern form: ₂F₁(1/4,3/4;1;k²) − (k/4)₂F₁(3/4,5/4;2;k²) = (1+k)^{−1/2}₂F₁(1/2,1/2;2;2k/(1+k)). The text never states it as a functional identity, only its value at k=1.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a minor documented instance of Euler-circle work containing Landen/Kummer-type quadratic transformations in substance. It is of historical interest only; the identity itself is classical.

missed.claim: The attempt to sum the series 'vicissim' through s and t and their ODE is left without reaching 2√2/π. The obstruction is that s and t individually diverge logarithmically at z=1.
missed.quote: Proposita autem vicissim hac serie, ejus valor ita investigari potest. Fiat k=zz
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Not mathematically new: the cancellation of logarithmic singularities is standard via connection formulas for ₂F₁. It is a historical note only.

deep.surprise_reason: All the computations are correct and the techniques are standard Eulerian ones. The only mildly notable features are the implicit quadratic hypergeometric transformation and the boundary series value 2√2/π, both classical in substance today. The page is apparently by J. A. Euler.
transcription_corrections: Previous page header attributes this section to '(J. A. Euler.)', so authorship is probably Johann Albrecht rather than Leonhard.
Transcription matches the image essentially; in the ds formula the image's t-term reads t(−4/z³ − 2z)dz, as transcribed (a stray mark precedes the minus).
